11740: Outrageous means something has crossed a line — it has gone so far beyond what is normal, acceptable, or expected that it causes a strong reaction in people. That reaction could be anger, disbelief, shock, or sometimes even laughter or delight. The word is always about extremity. Something outrageous is never mildly strange — it is dramatically, strikingly, undeniably extreme.

"Outrageous" carries two related but distinct flavors depending on context.

Meaning 1 — Shocking, Unacceptable, or Morally Wrong (Negative)

This is the primary and most common meaning. When something is outrageous in this sense, it is so unreasonable, unfair, offensive, or wrong that it shocks people and makes them angry or deeply upset. It violates people's sense of what is right, decent, or fair.

Examples:

  • "The company charged ₹50,000 for a simple repair. The price was outrageous."

Here, the price is so unreasonably high that it goes beyond what any fair-minded person would accept.

  • "He lied to the court and blamed an innocent man. It was an outrageous act."

The behavior is not just bad — it is deeply shocking and morally wrong.

  • "The minister made an outrageous claim that he had never taken bribes, despite the evidence."

The claim is so far from the truth, and said so boldly, that people are stunned by the audacity of it.

  • "The conditions in that prison were outrageous — no food, no water, no medical care."

The situation is so far below basic standards of human decency that it provokes strong moral outrage.

In this meaning, "outrageous" often carries a sense of injustice or violation. You use it when something makes you think: "This should not be happening. This is completely unacceptable."

Meaning 2 — Wildly Bold, Extravagant, or Over-the-Top (Neutral to Positive)

In a lighter, more informal sense, "outrageous" can describe something that is wildly dramatic, flamboyant, or extreme in a way that is entertaining, funny, or attention-grabbing — without necessarily being morally wrong. Here, the word carries a sense of playful exaggeration.

Examples:

  • "She showed up to the wedding in an outrageous purple sequin suit."

The outfit is extremely bold and attention-grabbing — probably not offensive, just wildly dramatic.

  • "His outrageous sense of humor had everyone in tears of laughter."

His humor is wild, extreme, boundary-pushing — but in a way that entertains people.

  • "That film has the most outrageous plot twist I have ever seen."

The twist is so unexpected and dramatic that it floors the audience — in a good or at least memorable way.

  • "She made an outrageous bet — she said she'd shave her head if the team lost."

The bet is wildly dramatic and extreme, but in a fun, daring way.

In this meaning, "outrageous" often carries a tone of amusement or admiration for boldness. It's used when something makes you think: "This is so extreme it's almost funny" or "Wow, that takes guts."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

The meaning depends almost entirely on tone and context.

  • If the sentence is about something unfair, harmful, morally wrong, or deeply unreasonable — it's the negative meaning.
  • If the sentence is about something bold, flashy, wild, or entertainingly extreme — it's the positive/neutral meaning.
  • Sometimes the same sentence can be ambiguous without more context. For example: "Her speech was outrageous" — this could mean it was shocking and offensive, or it could mean it was wildly bold and memorable.

A useful trick: pay attention to how the speaker feels. If they're angry or morally troubled, it's the negative sense. If they're amused or impressed, it's the lighter sense.

"Outrageous" is a strong adjective. It is not used for minor surprises or small inconveniences. It implies a high degree of extremity.

Consider this scale:

  • Unusual → Surprising → Shocking → Outrageous

When you call something outrageous, you are making a strong statement — that it is at the far end of what people can accept or believe.

The feeling of something being outrageous usually comes from one or more of these:

  • It violates a norm — it breaks an unspoken or explicit rule about how people behave, how things should be priced, or what is fair.
  • It exceeds expectations dramatically — whether in a bad way (like a terrible injustice) or in a wild way (like an extreme fashion choice).
  • It provokes a strong emotional reaction — anger, disbelief, moral shock, or amused disbelief.

For the negative meaning (shocking, unacceptable):
shocking, scandalous, appalling, disgraceful, unconscionable, monstrous, egregious, intolerable, offensive, unacceptable, preposterous

For the positive/neutral meaning (wildly bold or extreme):
wild, extravagant, flamboyant, over-the-top, audacious, extreme, outlandish, theatrical, larger-than-life

Opposite of the negative meaning:
reasonable, fair, acceptable, decent, appropriate, justified

Opposite of the positive/neutral meaning:
restrained, understated, modest, conservative, subtle

"Outrageous" is frequently used with certain nouns. Here are the most natural combinations:

  • outrageous behavior — conduct that shocks or offends people
  • outrageous price / outrageous cost — unreasonably high price
  • outrageous claim / outrageous lie — a statement so bold or false it shocks people
  • outrageous demand — an unreasonable request
  • outrageous outfit / outrageous costume — an extremely bold or dramatic way of dressing
  • outrageous sense of humor — humor that is wildly bold or boundary-pushing
  • outrageous suggestion — an idea so extreme or wrong that people are shocked by it

• "It is outrageous that a hospital turned away a patient because they couldn't pay." (morally wrong, unacceptable)
  • "The tax on basic food items is outrageous in this country." (shockingly unreasonable)
  • "His outrageous dancing at the office party became the talk of the company for weeks." (wildly bold, entertaining)
  • "She made the most outrageous cake for the birthday — five tiers, covered in edible glitter and sparklers." (wonderfully extreme)
  • "I find it outrageous that he was never punished for what he did." (deeply unjust, morally shocking)

Outrageous means: so extreme that it goes beyond what people consider normal, fair, or acceptable — causing strong reactions of anger, disbelief, or sometimes, amused shock.

  • In its serious use: shockingly bad, deeply unfair, morally unacceptable.
  • In its playful use: wildly bold, dramatically extreme, entertainingly over-the-top.

The word always points to something at the far edge of normal — something that makes people stop and say: "I can't believe this."
11741:
Outré means so bizarre, exaggerated, or unconventional that it goes beyond what most people consider acceptable or normal — often to the point of being shocking, eyebrow-raising, or just wildly "too much."

Think of it this way: if "unusual" is one step away from normal, and "eccentric" is two steps away, outré is three steps away — so far outside the ordinary that it makes people stop and stare.
What It Really Means in Plain Terms

The word captures a specific kind of strangeness. Something outré isn't just different or quirky — it's so extreme, so over-the-top, or so far outside social norms that it almost feels like a deliberate violation of what's expected. There's an element of extravagance to it. It's the difference between an artist who uses unusual colours and an artist who paints entirely in motor oil while wearing a wedding dress on a rooftop.

Crucially, outré applies to things that feel deliberately exaggerated or consciously excessive, not just accidentally odd. The strangeness has a kind of theatrical boldness to it.
What Can Be Described as Outré

The word is flexible and can describe many things:

  • Behaviour — Someone who shows up to a formal dinner and begins reciting poetry loudly to strangers has outré behaviour.
  • Appearance or fashion — A costume made entirely of peacock feathers and mirrors is outré.
  • Ideas or opinions — A politician who seriously proposes abolishing the concept of weekdays holds outré views.
  • Art, writing, or style — A novel written entirely from the perspective of a doorknob, with no plot, could be described as outré.
  • Performances — A stage show where the performer eats their own set design is outré.
The Tone of the Word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

This is important to understand, because outré is not a fixed insult or compliment — its emotional colour depends entirely on who is using it and in what context.

  • Used critically, it implies that something has gone too far — it's excessive, tasteless, or inappropriately shocking. "His outré behaviour at the funeral appalled everyone."
  • Used admiringly, especially in art, fashion, or creative circles, it can signal that something is thrillingly bold and boundary-breaking. "Her outré designs made her the talk of Paris."
  • Used neutrally, it simply observes that something is extremely unconventional without passing clear judgment. "The film had an outré, almost surreal quality that divided audiences."

The word has a slightly raised eyebrow built into it — there's always a sense of "this is a lot" — but whether that's good or bad is left to context.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Many words describe strangeness, but outré occupies a precise spot among them. Here's how to distinguish it:

  • Weird / strange — General and vague. Something weird is just not normal. Outré is much more specific: it's extreme, theatrical, and exceeds social norms in a noticeable way.
  • Eccentric — Eccentric describes a person who has unusual habits or personality quirks, often charmingly so. An eccentric professor might wear mismatched socks and talk to their houseplants. That's endearing. Outré implies something more extreme and attention-commanding than mere eccentricity.
  • Bizarre — Bizarre is close to outré but tends to emphasise pure strangeness and inexplicability. Something bizarre makes you think "what on earth is this?" Something outré makes you think "this has gone too far" or "this is shockingly over the top."
  • Flamboyant — Flamboyant focuses on showiness and love of attention. A person can be flamboyant in a fun, harmless way. Outré goes further — it doesn't just stand out, it transgresses.
  • Unconventional — Mild and neutral. Unconventional just means not following usual conventions. Outré implies crossing a line that unconventional doesn't even approach.

The key distinction: outré always implies an excess that pushes past normal boundaries — not just something different, but something that most people would feel is too much.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Outré is a formal, literary, and somewhat sophisticated word. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Art, fashion, and cultural criticism
  • Literary writing and novels
  • Formal essays or reviews
  • Intellectual conversation

You would not typically hear someone say it casually in everyday conversation. If your friend does something odd, you'd probably just say it was "wild" or "bizarre." If a theatre critic is reviewing an experimental play, they might call it outré. It carries a slightly elegant, refined flavour — using it shows a certain verbal sophistication.

• "The artist's outré installations — including a room filled entirely with live bees — disturbed and fascinated in equal measure."
  • "Even by the standards of that eccentric era, his outré lifestyle set him apart from his contemporaries."
  • "She had an outré sense of fashion: floor-length velvet capes, towering hats, and shoes shaped like animals."
  • "The politician's outré proposal to replace all currency with handwritten IOUs was dismissed within hours."
  • "What strikes readers most is the novel's outré humour — jokes so dark and strange they feel almost dangerous."

If you need to lock the meaning in memory with a single sentence:

Outré describes something so extravagantly unconventional, exaggerated, or shocking that it clearly exceeds what most people would consider normal or acceptable — and it always carries the sense of a line being crossed, whether admirably or scandalously.
11742:
Outset means the beginning or the very start of something — the earliest point in time when something begins.

That's the whole idea. If something happens "at the outset," it happens right at the beginning, before anything else has unfolded.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Think of any situation that has a clear starting point — a project, a journey, a conversation, a career, a problem. The outset is that very first moment when the thing begins.

  • "At the outset of the journey, everyone was excited."

→ Right at the beginning of the journey, before it had really gotten started, everyone was excited.

  • "From the outset, the plan seemed risky."

→ From the very beginning — even before anything went wrong — the plan already seemed risky.

  • "Let me make one thing clear at the outset."

→ Before we go any further, before we get into the details, let me say this one thing first.
The Two Phrases You'll Almost Always See It In

"Outset" almost never stands alone. It lives inside two fixed phrases:

1. "At the outset" — meaning at the beginning

"At the outset, nobody knew how serious the situation was."

2. "From the outset" — meaning from the very beginning, all along

"From the outset, she knew this job would be challenging."

The phrase "from the outset" carries a subtle but important extra feeling: it implies that something was true the whole time, starting from day one. When someone says "This was a mistake from the outset," they mean it was a mistake from the very first moment — not just later on.

You might wonder: "Isn't this just the same as 'beginning' or 'start'?" Mostly, yes — but there are small differences worth knowing.

Outset vs. Beginning/Start:
These three words all point to the same general idea, but "outset" is slightly more formal and deliberate in tone. You'd see it more in written English, speeches, or careful explanations than in casual conversation. You wouldn't typically say "The outset of the movie was boring" the way you'd say "The beginning of the movie was boring." "Outset" tends to be used when you want to set the stage or make a point about where something started.

Outset vs. Onset:
This one trips people up. Onset usually refers to the beginning of something negative or unwanted — like the onset of a disease, the onset of winter, the onset of a crisis. Outset, on the other hand, is neutral — it can describe the start of anything, good or bad.

There is a subtle but interesting quality to "outset." It often implies that you are looking back at the beginning from a later point. When someone says "We should have known from the outset," they are standing at some later moment and casting their eyes back to where it all started. This gives the word a slightly reflective or evaluative quality — as if the speaker is measuring where things began against how they turned out.
A Few More Examples Across Different Contexts

• "The rules were explained at the outset so there would be no confusion later."
  • "From the outset of their friendship, they had a deep understanding of each other."
  • "The project was underfunded from the outset, which led to its failure."
  • "I want to thank everyone at the outset for being here today."
  • "It was clear from the very outset that negotiations would be difficult."

(Note: "From the very outset" is a common intensified form, where "very" adds extra emphasis to how early something was true.)

Outset = the beginning. You'll almost always see it in the phrases "at the outset" (at the start) or "from the outset" (from the very beginning). It's slightly formal, neutral in tone, and often carries a sense of looking back at where something first began.
11743:
To outshine someone or something means to be so much better, more impressive, or more brilliant that the other person or thing looks dull or less significant by comparison.

Think of it this way: when the sun rises, the stars don't disappear — but they seem to disappear, because the sun's light is so powerful it drowns out their glow completely. That relationship — where one thing is so bright it makes everything else fade — is the heart of what "outshine" means.

This verb works on two levels, and both are correct and common:

1. The Literal Meaning (about actual light)

When one source of light is so much brighter than another that the other one can barely be noticed.

"The stadium floodlights outshine every streetlamp around it."

Here, you are talking about real, physical brightness.

2. The Figurative Meaning (about people, talent, and performance)

This is by far the more common and important use. When a person — through their talent, skill, beauty, intelligence, charm, or achievement — performs so impressively that others around them look ordinary or lesser in comparison, that person outshines the others.

"At the school talent show, Maya outshone every other performer with her singing."

Maya didn't make the others disappear. They were still there, still performing. But Maya was so good that, in comparison, the others seemed much less impressive.
The Hidden Logic of the Word

Here is something important to understand: outshining is always relative. You cannot outshine in isolation. You always outshine something or someone. The word only makes sense when there is a comparison happening.

Also — and this is subtle but important — the person being outshone is not necessarily bad or weak. They might be very good. But the person outshining them is simply better, or more noticeable, in that particular moment or context.

"The veteran actors were talented, but the young newcomer outshone them all at the awards ceremony."

The veterans are still talented. The newcomer just shone brighter.

The word carries a sense of effortless superiority — it feels less aggressive than words like "defeat" or "crush," but it still implies a clear winner and a clear loser in terms of impressiveness. It is often used to describe someone who naturally stands out rather than someone who fights to win.

It can sometimes carry a slightly uncomfortable undertone — being outshone can feel like being overshadowed or upstaged, which is not always a pleasant experience for the person on the receiving end.
Common Contexts Where You'll See It

• Performance & talent: "Her debut novel outshone everything else published that year."
  • Beauty & appearance: "The bride was stunning, but her maid of honor somehow outshone her in the photos."
  • Academic or professional achievement: "He outshone his colleagues by delivering results no one else could match."
  • Products & technology: "The new phone outshines its competitors in battery life and camera quality."
All the Verb Forms You'll Need

FormExample
Base"She will outshine everyone."
Third person (he/she/it)"He outshines all his rivals."
Past tense"She outshone everyone at the gala." (Note: not "outshined" — though "outshined" is sometimes seen, outshone is the standard and preferred past form.)
Present participle"She is outshining the competition."
Past participle"He has outshone every predecessor."

To outshine means to be so much more impressive, brilliant, or capable than others — in any quality, from literal brightness to talent to beauty — that by comparison, those others seem dim or ordinary.
11744:
When "outside" works as a preposition, it always sits directly before a noun or noun phrase. Its job is to tell you that something is beyond the boundary of that noun — not within it.

The core idea is this: imagine any boundary. It could be the walls of a room, the edge of a city, or even the invisible outer limit of someone's authority or knowledge. "Outside" places something on the far side of that boundary — beyond it, excluded from it.

This is the most literal use. Something is located beyond the physical edges of a place.

  • She waited outside the hospital.
    (Not inside the hospital — beyond its walls.)
  • They found a café outside the station.
    (Just beyond the station's boundary, not inside it.)
  • The car is parked outside the gate.
    (Beyond the gate, on the outer side.)

The pattern is always: outside + [place] = located beyond that place's boundary.
Meaning 2 — Beyond the limits of something abstract

This is where the word becomes far more powerful. "Outside" isn't just for physical places. You can also use it with abstract things — authority, knowledge, a budget, a law, a time period — to say something goes beyond the limits of those things.

Think of any abstract concept as having an invisible boundary — the outer edge of what it covers or includes. "Outside" places something beyond that edge.

  • This decision is outside my authority.
    (It goes beyond the boundaries of my authority. I have no power over it.)
  • Your question is outside my area of expertise.
    (The question goes beyond what I know about.)
  • The price is outside our budget.
    (The price exceeds the outer limit of what our budget allows.)
  • Their behaviour is outside the law.
    (Their behaviour goes beyond what the law permits — it breaks the law.)
  • The meeting fell outside working hours.
    (It happened beyond the time period defined as "working hours.")

In every case, something is being pushed past the limit, scope, or range of something else.
Meaning 3 — "Outside of": apart from, or except for

When you use "outside of" (with "of" after it), it carries a related but slightly different meaning: apart from, or other than, or except for.

Here, you are not describing a physical or abstract boundary. Instead, you are setting something aside and talking about what remains once it is excluded.

  • Outside of work, she loves painting.
    (Apart from work — if we put work aside — she loves painting.)
  • Outside of a few close friends, nobody knew about it.
    (Except for a few close friends, nobody knew.)
  • Outside of that one problem, everything went smoothly.
    (Other than that one problem, everything was fine.)

An important distinction: This "except for / apart from" meaning belongs specifically to "outside of" (with "of"). Using just "outside" alone — without "of" — does not naturally carry this sense in standard English. So if you want to say "apart from," use "outside of."
How to tell "outside" the preposition from "outside" the adverb

This is a very common point of confusion, so here is a clean rule:

  • If "outside" is followed by a noun or noun phrase → it is a preposition.
    She sat outside the café. (the noun "the café" follows it)
  • If "outside" stands alone with nothing after it → it is an adverb.
    She sat outside. (nothing follows it)

Both sentences are perfectly correct, but "outside" is doing two different grammatical jobs.
The unifying idea — hold all three meanings together

Every meaning of "outside" as a preposition is about a boundary. Something exists on the far side of that boundary.

  • With a physical place, the boundary is its walls or edges.
  • With an abstract concept — authority, knowledge, a budget, the law, a time period — the boundary is the outer limit of what that concept covers.
  • With "outside of" meaning "apart from," you are mentally stepping past one specific thing and looking at everything else beyond it.

Cross the boundary → you are outside.

These are set phrases built on this preposition. Knowing them will make reading and listening much easier.

Outside the box — beyond conventional, standard thinking; creative or unconventional.
We need to think outside the box to solve this problem.

Outside the law — beyond what the law permits; illegal.
Their activities were clearly outside the law.

Outside someone's comfort zone — beyond the range of situations a person feels comfortable with.
Public speaking is well outside her comfort zone.

Outside the scope (of something) — beyond the boundary of what something is meant to cover.
That topic is outside the scope of this course.

Outside of that — apart from that; other than that (used informally to introduce an exception).
There were a few delays, but outside of that, the trip was perfect.
A final summary to anchor everything

Boundary typeExampleWhat it means

When the boundary is physical, "outside" tells you where something is located — beyond the walls or edges of a place. When the boundary is abstract, "outside" tells you that something exceeds or falls beyond the reach, limit, or scope of a concept. When you use "outside of", you are marking an exception — setting one thing aside and referring to everything beyond it.

That is the complete picture. The word always carries the same heart: a boundary exists, and something is on the far side of it.
11745:
An outside chance means a very small but real possibility that something will happen. When you say someone has an "outside chance," you mean they are unlikely to succeed — but it's not completely impossible either.

Picture a scale from 0% to 100%. "No chance at all" lives at 0%. "A very good chance" sits around 70–80%. An "outside chance" hovers somewhere around 5–15%. Low, yes — but it's not zero. That tiny gap between zero and low is exactly what this idiom lives in.

The word "outside" here has nothing to do with the outdoors or a physical location. It is used figuratively to mean beyond what is normally expected. The possibility is so small that it falls "outside" the range of what you'd typically count on.

The most widely accepted origin of this idiom is horse racing. In a race, the horse running on the outer lane has a longer distance to cover than horses on the inner lanes. That extra distance made the outer horse harder to back as a winner. So an "outside horse" was the unlikely contender — possible, but not the favourite. Over time, "outside chance" migrated into everyday language to describe any situation where the odds are against you, but you haven't been knocked out of the running entirely.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The idiom usually appears in two structures:

"There's an outside chance that…" — used when talking about a situation or event.

  • "There's an outside chance that it will snow in July." (Wildly unlikely but not scientifically impossible.)
  • "There's an outside chance the flight will depart on time given the delays."

"Someone has an outside chance of…" — used when talking about a person's likelihood of achieving something.

  • "She has an outside chance of winning the championship." (She's not the favourite, but she could still pull it off.)
  • "The team has an outside chance of finishing in third place."

Notice how in every case, the sentence quietly acknowledges two things at once: probably not, and but maybe.
The Tone — Honest, But Not Crushing

One of the most important things to understand about this idiom is its emotional tone. It is realistic without being cruel. It doesn't slam the door shut — it simply says the door is barely open.

This makes it especially useful in contexts where you want to be truthful without completely extinguishing hope. A news anchor covering an election might say, "The challenger has an outside chance of defeating the incumbent." That sentence is fair to the facts while still treating the challenger with dignity. It's not saying "give up" — it's saying "the numbers aren't on your side, but stranger things have happened."

Many learners mistakenly treat "outside chance" as meaning "no chance." This is wrong, and it's an important distinction.

"No chance" = zero possibility. Done. Impossible.
"Outside chance" = very low possibility. Unlikely, but still alive.

If you say to a friend, "You have an outside chance of getting that job," you are actually offering them a small encouragement. You are saying they're in the running, even if they're not the frontrunner. If you mean to say they have zero hope, you should instead say "no chance" or "not a chance."

Never use "outside chance" to describe something truly impossible. Reserve it for situations that are unlikely but within the realm of the possible.
How It Compares to Similar Expressions

English has several idioms that cover the same neighbourhood of meaning, but each has its own shade.

"A slim chance" and "a remote chance" are the closest cousins to "outside chance." All three mean roughly the same thing — a small but real possibility. You can swap them in most sentences without changing the meaning significantly. "There's a slim chance of rain" and "there's an outside chance of rain" are nearly identical.

"A long shot" also means something unlikely to succeed. The difference is that "long shot" often carries a slight sense of boldness or daring — it's a bet you make knowing the odds are against you. "Winning that contract would be a long shot, but let's try." It sometimes implies effort and risk, while "outside chance" is more neutral and observational.

"A fighting chance" is noticeably more optimistic than "outside chance." A fighting chance means you have a genuine, real possibility of succeeding — especially if you work hard. It implies more hope. "If we train hard, we have a fighting chance of winning." An outside chance, by contrast, leans toward the doubtful side.

"Fat chance" is a trap for learners. It sounds like it should mean "a large chance," but it's completely sarcastic and actually means no chance at all. "Fat chance he'll apologise!" means he absolutely will not apologise. Never confuse this with "outside chance."

Here's a rough sense of how they line up, from most hopeful to least hopeful:

Good chance → Fighting chance → Outside / Slim / Remote chance → Long shot → Fat chance / No chance at all.
Register — Who Uses It and Where?

"Outside chance" is flexible. It appears in sports commentary, journalism, casual conversation, and formal writing. It's not slang, and it's not stiff or old-fashioned. A sports journalist, a politician, a scientist discussing probabilities, or your neighbour chatting over the fence — all of them could naturally use this expression without it sounding out of place.

An outside chance = a very small but genuine possibility that something could happen, even though it most likely won't.

Unlikely? Yes. Impossible? No. That thin line between those two ideas is exactly where this idiom lives.
11746: "Outskirts" refers to the outer areas or edges of a city or town — the parts that sit at the boundary between the main urban area and the open land (or countryside) beyond it. Think of a city as a circle. The busy center with its offices, markets, and dense buildings is the heart. As you move away from that center toward the boundary of the city, you gradually enter the outskirts — the fringes, the edges, the less-developed rim of the place.

This is one of the most important things to know about this word: "outskirts" is always used in the plural form. There is no singular "outskirt." You will never correctly say "the outskirt of the city." It is always "the outskirts of the city." This is simply how the word works in English, and there are no exceptions.
What the outskirts actually look like

The outskirts are not a sharp line — they are a zone, a gradual transition. As you travel from the center of a city toward its outskirts, you notice the buildings getting fewer and more spread out, the streets getting quieter, more open land appearing, and the feeling of the busy city starting to fade. You might see:

  • Factories and warehouses (industrial areas are often placed here, where land is cheaper)
  • Smaller houses with larger plots of land
  • New housing developments under construction
  • Fields, forests, or open space beginning to appear
  • Fewer shops, restaurants, and public services

The outskirts are neither fully "in the city" nor fully "outside" it. They are the in-between zone.
How it is used in sentences
The word "outskirts" almost always appears with the preposition "on" and is followed by "of" and a place name. The standard pattern is:

Here are examples:

  • "She lives on the outskirts of Delhi." → She lives near the edge of Delhi, not in the city center.
  • "They built the new airport on the outskirts of the town." → The airport is at the edge of the town, away from the main area.
  • "The factory was located on the outskirts." → (Here, the place is understood from context, so "of [place]" is dropped.)
  • "We drove through the outskirts before reaching the city center." → They passed through the edge areas first.

You can also say someone or something is "in the outskirts," but "on the outskirts" is far more common and natural.
The feeling and connotation of the word

"Outskirts" carries a mild sense of distance from the main action. When something is "on the outskirts," it implies it is away from the center of life, activity, and convenience. This can be neutral, slightly negative, or even positive depending on context:

  • Neutral: "The new hospital is on the outskirts of the city." (Just stating location.)
  • Slightly negative: "He felt isolated, living on the outskirts, far from everything." (Implying loneliness or inconvenience.)
  • Positive: "They chose a house on the outskirts for the peace and quiet." (Implying a preference for calm over bustle.)

The word itself does not judge — the tone comes from the sentence around it.
How it differs from similar words

It helps to know how "outskirts" compares to words that seem close in meaning:

  • Suburbs — Suburbs are specifically residential neighborhoods outside the city center, often planned communities where families live. Suburbs are one type of outskirts. But "outskirts" is broader — it includes industrial zones, farmland on the city's edge, and any peripheral area, not just residential ones.
  • Edge — "Edge" is a very general word (you can talk about the edge of a table). "Outskirts" is specifically about the edge of a settlement (city, town, village).
  • Periphery — This word is more formal and can be used both literally and abstractly (e.g., "on the periphery of society"). "Outskirts" is more concrete and almost always refers to physical geography.
  • Boundary / Border — These refer to a line — the exact point where something ends. "Outskirts" refers to a zone or area, not a single line.
Can it be used for things other than cities?

Almost always, "outskirts" refers to the edges of a town, city, or village — a human settlement. You would not normally say "the outskirts of a forest" or "the outskirts of a country." It is anchored to places where people live or have built things.

Occasionally, you might see it used loosely in a figurative way (e.g., "on the outskirts of polite society"), but this is uncommon and somewhat literary. In everyday use, it is always about the physical edges of a place.

"Outskirts" = the outer, peripheral areas at the edges of a city or town, forming a transitional zone between the urban center and the open land beyond. Always plural. Always used with "on" + "of." Refers to a zone, not a sharp line. Slightly implies distance from the main center of activity.
11747:
When someone is outspoken, they say what they truly think — directly, boldly, and without holding back — even when their opinion might be uncomfortable, unpopular, or controversial. An outspoken person does not stay silent just to avoid conflict or to keep others happy. They speak up, speak clearly, and speak honestly.

Think of it this way: most people have opinions they keep to themselves because they fear judgment, awkwardness, or disagreement. An outspoken person feels no such fear. They will say the thing that others are only thinking.

Three qualities always live inside this word:

Directness. An outspoken person does not hint, beat around the bush, or soften their message into meaninglessness. They get straight to the point.

Courage. Being outspoken is not simply about talking a lot. A person who chatters endlessly about safe, harmless topics is not outspoken — they are just talkative. What makes someone outspoken is the willingness to voice opinions that carry some risk — the risk of disagreement, backlash, or social discomfort.

Honesty. Outspoken people say what they genuinely believe. It is not performance. It is not exaggeration for attention. It is their real, unfiltered view.
The Feeling of the Word — Positive or Negative?

"Outspoken" is mostly a positive or neutral word, but the feeling it carries depends on your point of view.

If you admire the quality of speaking truth fearlessly, you see an outspoken person as brave, refreshing, and trustworthy. You feel you always know where they stand.

If you find that quality uncomfortable or disruptive, you might see the same person as blunt, harsh, or difficult. Too outspoken can feel like a lack of tact or sensitivity.

The word itself does not judge. It simply describes. Whether it feels like a compliment or a quiet criticism depends entirely on context and tone.

Like most adjectives, outspoken exists on a scale. A person can be mildly outspoken — meaning they occasionally voice a bold opinion when the moment feels right. Or they can be fiercely outspoken — meaning they almost always say what they think, in nearly every situation, regardless of the audience or the consequences.

You will often see it paired with intensifiers to show this range:

  • "She is quite outspoken."
  • "He is famously outspoken."
  • "She is refreshingly outspoken."
  • "He is notoriously outspoken."
Who or What Can Be Described as Outspoken?

Almost always, this word describes a person. You use it to describe someone's general personality or communication style — something consistent about how they are, not just a single thing they said once.

Common examples:

  • An outspoken critic — someone who publicly and fearlessly attacks what they find wrong or flawed.
  • An outspoken activist — someone who boldly speaks up for a cause, especially when it is unpopular.
  • An outspoken leader — one who does not hide behind vague, careful language.
  • An outspoken opponent — someone who openly and actively disagrees.

You would not normally call a single remark "outspoken." You call a person outspoken because it describes their character. However, you can occasionally describe a speech, statement, or stance as outspoken if it reflects remarkable boldness or directness — for example, "an outspoken defense of the accused."

Here are sentences that show the word working naturally:

  • "She has always been outspoken about the need for better working conditions, even when her managers disagreed."
  • "He is an outspoken critic of the government's handling of the crisis."
  • "What I love about her is that she's outspoken — you never have to guess what she's thinking."
  • "The outspoken senator refused to water down his remarks, despite pressure from his party."
  • "As a student, she was already outspoken, always challenging ideas that didn't make sense to her."

It is important not to confuse outspoken with words that seem similar but mean something different.

Outspoken is not the same as rude. A rude person is disrespectful or offensive. An outspoken person is direct and honest, but directness alone is not rudeness. Many outspoken people are also kind and respectful — they simply do not hide their views.

Outspoken is not the same as talkative. A talkative person talks a lot. An outspoken person says meaningful, bold things — but they might not even talk that much. Quantity of speech is not the point. Courage of speech is.

Outspoken is not the same as aggressive. Aggressive speech attacks, intimidates, or tries to dominate. Outspoken speech simply states an honest view without softening it. The intent is different.

Understanding what a word is not can sharpen your understanding of what it is. The opposites of outspoken include:

  • Reserved — someone who keeps their thoughts and feelings to themselves.
  • Reticent — someone reluctant or slow to speak, especially on sensitive matters.
  • Diplomatic — someone careful to phrase things in a way that avoids offending, often at the cost of full honesty.
  • Guarded — someone who is cautious and controlled about what they reveal.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you forget everything else, remember this: an outspoken person says what they truly think, even when it is not easy to say it. The heart of this word is fearless honesty. That is what makes someone outspoken — not volume, not aggression, not rudeness, but the quiet (or sometimes not-so-quiet) courage to speak the truth as they see it.
11748:
When something is outspread, it is stretched wide open or extended outward to its full extent — spread out in all directions, or to both sides, from a central point.

Think of an eagle soaring in the sky with both wings fully extended to their widest. Those wings are outspread. Nothing is folded, tucked, or held back. Everything is open and reaching outward.

"Outspread" describes the condition of something that has been:

  • fully unfolded and laid open, OR
  • extended or stretched wide in multiple directions

The key idea is maximum extension — whatever it is, it is spread to its fullest, not just slightly open or partially extended.

Wings

"The hawk glided silently with outspread wings."

The wings are fully stretched from the body outward — not folded, not mid-flap, but wide and still.

Arms

"She stood at the door with outspread arms, ready to embrace her child."

Both arms are extended wide open — the way you'd open your arms for a hug, or to welcome someone warmly.

Hands / Fingers

"He pressed his outspread hand against the window."

The fingers are spread apart, the palm is fully open — not clenched or curled.

A map or cloth or document

"The treasure map lay outspread on the table."

The map is fully unfolded and laid flat — open across the surface, nothing rolled or folded.

Branches or roots

"The outspread roots of the banyan tree covered the ground."

The roots stretch far and wide in all directions from the trunk.

"Outspread" is almost always a visual word. It paints a picture of something you can see extending outward. When you read it, your mind automatically forms an image of something open, wide, and reaching — like a fan fully opened, or a bird in full glide.

It often carries a sense of stillness at the moment of full extension — the wings are spread and held there, the arms are opened wide and waiting. It is not describing a movement (like spreading wings), but a state (the wings are already spread and held open).

• It does not mean scattered or messy (like papers thrown around randomly).
  • It does not mean small or partial — "outspread" always implies a wide, full extension.
  • It is not the same as simply "open." A door can be open just a little. But something outspread is open broadly and expansively.

In writing, "outspread" often carries a tone of openness, generosity, welcome, or freedom. Outspread arms suggest a warm welcome. Outspread wings suggest freedom and soaring. Even outspread roots suggest strength quietly reaching everywhere.

It is a word used more in formal, literary, or descriptive writing than in everyday casual speech. You're more likely to read it in a novel, a poem, or a nature documentary script than to hear it in normal conversation.

What it meansFully stretched out or extended wide open
What it describesWings, arms, hands, maps, branches, fabric — anything that can be spread wide
The core imageSomething fully open and reaching outward, held at maximum extension
Tone in writingOften suggests openness, freedom, or welcome; used in formal/literary contexts

In one sentence: "Outspread" means fully extended and spread wide open — like an eagle's wings held out to both sides at their maximum reach.
11749:
To outstay something or someone means to stay longer than you should, or longer than someone else does.

The word is built from two parts: out- (meaning "beyond" or "more than") + stay. So to outstay is literally to "out-stay" — to stay past a certain point or beyond someone else.

1. To outstay a time limit or permitted period

This means to remain somewhere beyond the time you were allowed or expected to stay.

"The tourist outstayed his visa."

He stayed in the country after his visa had already expired. He was no longer legally permitted to be there, but he remained anyway.

2. To outstay someone else

This means to stay longer than another person — to still be there after they have already left.

"She outstayed all the other guests at the party."

Everyone else went home, but she was still there. She outlasted them all in terms of staying.
The most famous use: "outstay one's welcome"

By far the most common way you'll encounter this verb is in the phrase "outstay one's welcome." This is so widely used that it has become an idiom.

It means: to stay somewhere so long that your host no longer wants you there.

When you arrive somewhere as a guest, your host is happy to have you. But if you stay too long, their happiness fades. They may feel tired, inconvenienced, or simply ready for you to leave — but are too polite to say so. At that point, you have outstayed your welcome.

"We enjoyed visiting, but I felt we had outstayed our welcome when they started yawning and looking at the clock."

"A good guest knows when to leave and never outstays their welcome."

The key feeling in this phrase is overstaying — pushing past the natural or comfortable end point of a visit, to the point where your presence has become a burden rather than a pleasure.

It is always transitive — meaning it must have an object. You don't just "outstay." You outstay something: your welcome, your visa, a competitor, the other guests.

It almost always carries a negative connotation. Even in sense 2 (staying longer than others), there's often a hint of stubbornness or refusal to leave — though context matters. In a competitive setting, outstaying your rivals can be seen positively:

"She outstayed her rivals in the negotiation, refusing to budge until the deal was signed."

Here it means she persisted and endured longer than others did — a kind of victory. But even so, the word carries the flavor of pushing beyond a natural endpoint.

SituationWhat "outstay" means

Actually, skipping the table as requested.

Think of "outstay" as a verb about crossing a line in time — staying past when you should have left, whether that line is set by a visa, a social expectation, or simply the moment when others have gone. The most essential phrase to remember is outstay one's welcome, because that is where the word lives most naturally in everyday English, and it perfectly captures the heart of what the verb means: staying so long that you wear out your welcome.
